extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of scientific method; investigators and philosophers of science
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and evaluative rules for forming and testing causal inferences in empirical science, focusing on the Methods of Agreement, Difference, Concomitant Variations, their combinations, and the complications introduced by plurality and intermixture of causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Agreement (use as suggestive, not definitive)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Method of Agreement: when varied cases all contain circumstance A and all show effect a, we may suppose A is connected with a — either as cause or as another effect of the same cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Method of Agreement is “of no real value” when the number of compared instances is small because of the possibility of plurality of causes; it yields at most a slight probability unless instances are very numerous and sufficiently various. Its proper role is to suggest hypotheses to be tested by the Method of Difference or by deduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Difference (gives rigorous induction)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Method of Difference: if B C gives b c, and A B C gives a b c, then A is either the cause of a or an indispensable part of its cause in that instance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method of Difference is free from the characteristic imperfection of the Method of Agreement arising from plurality of causes; two instances (one positive and one negative) are sufficient for the most complete and rigorous induction for that case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint Method of Agreement and Difference (Indirect Method of Difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: The joint method supposes instances in which a occurs agree only in containing A, and instances in which a does not occur agree only in not containing A, thereby making A the only possible cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This joint method avoids the imperfection of simple Agreement. It is one of the most powerful inductive tools (after Direct Method of Difference), especially in sciences relying on pure observation; it combines affirmative and negative premises to render conclusions stronger.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of Concomitant Variations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Method of Concomitant Variations is one of the four methods of observation and experiment (alongside Agreement, Difference, and Deduction) and plays a large part in establishing empirical laws in complex cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concomitant Variations help where quantities vary together; they are part of the empirical toolkit (e.g., in astronomical reasoning) but should be used alongside other methods and deduction for proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Deduction to untangle intermixture of effects
rubrics_metrics.description: When causes interfere with one another and effects are intermingled or modify each other (composition of causes), Deduction is the instrument 'adequate to unravel the complexities'—experimental methods mainly supply premises and verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where composition or intermixture of effects makes direct induction inadequate, deductive reasoning (from known laws and premises) is necessary to separate and identify component causal contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware Plurality of Causes
rubrics_metrics.description: An effect may sometimes arise from A, sometimes from B; many causes may produce the same phenomenon. This plurality renders the Method of Agreement uncertain unless rebutted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To guard against plurality of causes, multiply and vary instances or apply the Method of Difference; ultimate assessment of how many instances suffice relates to probability theory. Do not rely on agreement over a small set of cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of Negative Instances (exclude antecedents)
rubrics_metrics.description: The negative premise (instances where phenomenon does not occur) is especially valuable because Agreement applied to negative instances is free from the characteristic imperfection affecting affirmative Agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although negative instances are often harder to obtain/exhaust, they are essential: showing that all non-occurrences share the absence of A is powerful evidence that A is necessary for the phenomenon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety not mere number of instances matters
rubrics_metrics.description: The tendency of unscientific inquirers is to rely on the mere mass of experience; mere number is important only because it helps rebut plurality of causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeatedly adding instances that differ only in points already known immaterial adds nothing. Vary circumstances to eliminate alternative antecedents; a single discriminating instance that excludes an antecedent can be more valuable than many similar ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeat identical trials first to ensure factual accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: It is necessary to assure ourselves, by repetition of the observation or experiment, that no error has been committed concerning the individual facts observed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before varying circumstances to probe causal structure, repeat the same experiment sufficiently to ensure errors in individual facts have been ruled out; only then is varying instances informative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental control to remove confounders (example: experiments in vacuo)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparent variation from a true law (e.g., air resistance affecting falling bodies) can be cleared up by experiments (e.g., in vacuo) that remove the disturbing circumstance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design experiments that eliminate suspected interfering conditions to reveal the underlying law; targeted experimental manipulations can transform suggestive Agreement into rigorous proof by Difference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish kinds of compound/heteropathic effects (chemical vs dynamical vs mental)
rubrics_metrics.description: When concurrence of causes produces a new phenomenon (transformation) the new fact may be directly investigated by experiment (chemical composition); when the compound ceases to preserve component laws (heteropathic mental phenomena), discovery may require synthetic study of simple constituents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For chemical-like transformations, analyze the phenomenon and attempt reconstitution or decomposition (chemical analysis). For complex mental or dynamical compositions where constituents cannot be reproduced, study simple elements and experiment on their combinations to understand emergent effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of Causes often conceals individual causal laws
rubrics_metrics.description: When causes compound their effects, the separate effects may be intermingled, canceled, or summed so that the resulting phenomenon does not obviously display any single law's operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that fulfilled laws may be present as tendencies even when their observable effects are masked; analytic and deductive methods are often required to infer component contributions from the compound result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Express laws as tendencies, not absolute results
rubrics_metrics.description: All laws of causation, because of liability to be counteracted, require to be stated in words affirmative of tendencies only (e.g., 'tends to move'), not of actual results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formulate general propositions so they assert tendencies or conditional actions rather than absolute outcomes, to avoid pseudo-exceptions created by unmentioned concurrent causes; this improves nomenclature and avoids misleading 'exceptions to laws.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use joint empirical and deductive strategies for complex phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: The four inductive methods can supply premises and verification, but are often unequal to cope with intermixture of effects; deduction is needed to unravel complexities and link empirical generalizations to laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine careful observational/experimental work (Agreement, Difference, Concomitant Variations, controlled repetition) with deductive reasoning from known laws to establish causes and conditions of recurrence for complex, intermingled phenomena.
